title: His character, and loving him today
hook: His servant of ten years never once heard "Why did you do that?" You never met him, and he longed to meet you.

screens.text: **His servant of ten years never once heard "Why did you do that?"** You never met him. But long before you were born, he said he longed to meet believers like you.
**Ten years, no blame.** Anas served the Prophet ﷺ for ten years. In all that time, Anas said, he never once snapped at him or asked why he had or hadn't done something [Bukhari 6038].
bubbles: Aisha said he never struck a woman or a servant, and never took revenge for himself [Muslim 2328].

screens.prompt: His everyday character: did he do this, or not?

items.text: Helped with the work at home
items.why: Aisha said he kept busy serving his family until prayer time [Bukhari 676].

items.text: Asked a little boy how his pet bird was doing
items.why: He'd tease Anas's little brother kindly about his bird [Bukhari 6203].

items.text: Hit a servant who made mistakes
items.why: He never struck a servant or a woman [Muslim 2328].

screens.text: **Character was his message.** He said the best of you are those with the best character [Bukhari 3559]. Asked what he was like, Aisha said his character was the Qur'an [Muslim 746]. Allah told him: *"And indeed, you are of a great moral character"* [Q 68:4, Saheeh Intl.].
Forty-one episodes in five steps, and one more.

events.title: Born in Makkah
events.text: An orphan in the Year of the Elephant [IslamQA 147601].

events.title: "Read!"
events.text: At forty, revelation begins at Hira [Bukhari 3902].

events.title: The hijra
events.text: After thirteen years in Makkah, he moves to Madinah [Bukhari 3902; Bukhari 3934].

events.title: He dies at sixty-three
events.text: In Madinah, in Aisha's home [Muslim 2348; Yaqeen].

events.title: You
events.text: One of the believers he longed for, who believe without having seen him [Muslim 249].

screens.text: **He longed for you.** At a graveyard he said he wished he could see his brothers. Aren't we your brothers? his Companions asked. You are my Companions, he said. My brothers are those who haven't come yet [Muslim 249].
bubbles: He said he'd recognise them on the Day of Judgement by the bright marks of wudu on their faces, arms and legs [Muslim 249].

screens.prompt: When he said "my brothers" were those who hadn't come yet, who did he mean?

options.text: Believers who would come later and believe without seeing him, including you
options.feedback: Yes. Every convert who says the shahada today is one of the people he longed to meet.
Not quite. He meant believers yet to come, people who'd never see him [Muslim 249].
Not quite. He called them his Companions. His brothers were those still to come [Muslim 249].

screens.text: **Love that grows.** He said none of you truly believes until you love him more than your parents, your children and everyone [Bukhari 15]. That isn't a feelings test. Love grows by getting to know someone, and you've just spent forty-one episodes doing that.
bubbles: *"If you should love Allah, then follow me, [so] Allah will love you"* [Q 3:31, Saheeh Intl.]. Loving him looks like following him, one habit at a time.

screens.title: Three ways to love him today

steps.text: Send blessings on him. Allah and His angels do, and believers are asked to [Q 33:56]. Say *Allahumma salli 'ala Muhammad* (O Allah, send blessings on Muhammad) any time.
Slow down at the Salat Ibrahimiyya in your prayer. Those words are blessings on him, the ones he taught [Bukhari 3370].
Copy one piece of his character: help at home, be gentle with children, keep your words clean [Bukhari 676; Bukhari 6203; Bukhari 3559].

screens.done_text: He is *"an excellent pattern"* for anyone who hopes in Allah [Q 33:21, Saheeh Intl.].

screens.situation: Destiny loved learning his story, but she feels she's not a good enough Muslim to love the Prophet ﷺ. She still misses Fajr and still swears when she's stressed.

options.text: Start loving him now, and let that love pull her toward his habits, one at a time
options.feedback: Yes. Love comes first and grows into following. He grieved over what burdens his people [Q 9:128].

options.text: Wait to love him until she's fixed herself
options.feedback: Not quite. Nobody fixes themselves first. Loving him is part of how people change.

options.text: Decide she'll never be anything like him, so why try
options.feedback: Not quite. Nobody is like him. He longed for believers like her anyway [Muslim 249].

That's the end of the seerah track. His story ends here; yours with him is just beginning.

options.feedback: Not quite. He called them his Companions; his brothers were those still to come [Muslim 249].

check.prompt: According to Q 3:31, what does loving Allah look like?

options.feedback: Right. Follow him, and Allah will love you [Q 3:31]. One habit at a time.

options.feedback: Not quite. The verse ties love to following him, which grows step by step [Q 3:31].

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- Anas served him for ten years and was never once told "uff" or "why did you do that / why didn't you" [Bukhari 6038].
- He never struck a woman or a servant (except in battle) and never took revenge for himself [Muslim 2328; Bukhari 3560].
- He never spoke obscenely and said the best are those with the best character [Bukhari 3559]. Aisha said his character was the Qur'an [Muslim 746]. "And indeed, you are of a great moral character" [Q 68:4].
- He served his family at home [Bukhari 676]; he played kindly with Anas's little brother about his pet bird [Bukhari 6203].
- At a graveyard he said he longed to see his brothers: those who had not yet come; he would recognise them by the marks of wudu on their faces, arms and legs [Muslim 249].
- None truly believes until he loves the Prophet ﷺ more than his father, his children and all people [Bukhari 15]. Love of Allah means following him [Q 3:31]. Allah and His angels send blessings on him, and believers are told to [Q 33:56]; he taught the words (the Salat Ibrahimiyya) [Bukhari 3370; Days 26–27].
- He was sent as a mercy to the worlds [Q 21:107]; what burdens believers grieves him [Q 9:128]; he is an excellent pattern [Q 33:21].
- Life outline for the timeline: born about 570 [IslamQA 147601]; revelation at forty [Bukhari 3902]; hijra after thirteen years, 622 CE, year 1 of the calendar [Bukhari 3902; Bukhari 3934]; died at sixty-three in 632 CE [Muslim 2348; Yaqeen].

**Likely questions**
- *"How do I send blessings on him?"* The fullest form is the Salat Ibrahimiyya they already say in prayer [Bukhari 3370; Days 26–27]. Outside prayer, short forms like "Allahumma salli 'ala Muhammad" (O Allah, send blessings on Muhammad), or writing/saying ﷺ after his name. No fixed number is required here; any amount is good.
- *"How can I love someone I've never met?"* The same way you come to love any great person: by learning about him, seeing how he treated people, and following what he taught. He longed for people like them [Muslim 249]. Love grows; it isn't a test they fail.
- *"Do I have to love him more than my parents? That feels wrong."* Gently: Bukhari 15 describes the highest love, and it grows over time. Loving him never means loving family less; he taught kindness to parents and family. Don't make it a guilt test (Day 15 rule).
- *"What should I read next?"* Suggest the mentor and imam recommend a seerah book in the convert's language; offer to revisit any episode.
- *"What were his everyday habits?"* Keep to sourced ones: serving his family [Bukhari 676], gentleness with children [Bukhari 6203; Bukhari 5997], clean speech [Bukhari 3559], never hitting [Muslim 2328], loving the siwak [Bukhari 4449]. Specific sunnah practices and their rulings go to the masjid's teachers.

**Escalate:** questions about celebrating the Mawlid or specific forms of praise (imam); a convert who feels unworthy to the point of despair (mentor).

**Don't**
- Don't say "the Prophet ﷺ would be disappointed in you" or use him to shame (Day 15 rule).
- Don't treat Bukhari 15 as a feelings test or a threat.
- Don't describe his physical appearance or suggest picturing him.
- Don't give rulings on numbers of salawat or on contested practices.
